title: Lithium: Must it Be Dosed Twice a Day?
subtitle: A Frontier Psychiatrists' guest post
body_html:
I'm thrilled to have the opportunity to share other writers' work on human health. This newsletter has a name that I'll admit is misleading. It has psychiatrists, plural, in the name. My wife chose the name! It's a play on The Avalanches’ song. A scientist wrote the following piece, but he's not a biomedical scientist. He's a physicist! Yes, it's my friend joining us again. You may remember his prior articles, like his epic five-part series on lithium blood levels? It's available here:

Lithium I

Lithium II

Lithium III

Lithium IV

Lithium V

He also co-authored an academic paper, along with our mutual friend (who also has an excellent book called Conversations in Critical Psychiatry, which I am well overdue for reviewing— buy it on Amazon (affiliate link) and review it yourself now!)

Alex is a physicist and a psychiatric patient. He became very interested in the topic of lithium because it was a great treatment for him. He felt that the science around lithium was tremendously strong, but the clinical practice was not. This is a view I share. Thus, I'm thrilled to welcome Alex back to this newsletter for the following article on the topic of lithium. It's dosed twice a day…but should it be?

I'll share the punchline if you're too busy to read this article. No, it should probably be dosed just once a day. There, I saved you a whole article.

Do something worthwhile with your free time. Maybe call your mother? I'm sitting here, next to my mother, and she's laughing when I made that joke. Your mother will appreciate the time you spend with her, also. However, if you are in a circumstance where there are no promixal moms, you can feel free to read the rest of this article on lithium dosing. It’s a lifesaving treatment for depression. It’s also a great Nirvana song.

Alex’s note: This is one of the first articles I wrote about lithium. I never published it because, well, it has far too many quotes. Crossing the chasm of knowledge between physics and psychiatry wasn’t easy – initially, I had to rely on the psychiatric researchers to speak for me. Instead of rewriting the article, I thought it might be a useful resource for anyone out there faced with the challenge of reading academic literature for the first time (and for everyone else an interesting story).

When first faced with this task, it can feel overwhelming. Results, graphs, tables, and figures fly at you which you can barely comprehend. Something I wish someone had told me when I first started reviewing academic literature was that even if you know almost nothing about a subject, the fundamental research story is already told in the literature, if you know where to look.

It is important to note that spotting the story is merely the first step in (non-systematic) literature review. It helps you to pinpoint the papers to look at in more detail, to see if the results back up the claims made.

In a 2020 academic paper by Barroilhet et al. [1], the following assertive statement is made:

The common practice of dosing lithium multiple times daily is based on habit without any general rationale

Dr. Chris Aiken (of the remarkable Carlat Report) gives a similar statement in a 2020 Psychiatric Times article [2]:

Lithium is often dosed twice a day, but I think that’s out of convention rather than science

Scientific research almost always informs widely adopted conventions in psychiatry. In this case, there seem to be many sensible reasons why multiple daily dose regimens became common practice and why they are now being replaced by once-daily dosing regimens.

Two books by F.N. Johnson, The History of Lithium Therapy[3] and the Handbook of Lithium Therapy [4], provide much of the necessary information. The former describes one of the more significant factors that contributed to the adoption of Multiple Daily Dosing (MDD), the “kidney scare” of the late 1970s:

In 1977 two reports appeared which brought matters to a head: in these, Dr H. E. Hansen, together with Dr Amdisen, Dr J. Hestbech and other colleagues, drew attention to chronic functional and morphological changes which occurred in the kidney of patients after extended treatment with lithium. In particular, disturbancesin renal concentrating ability and glomerular sclerosis were found to be far more common in the lithium-treated patients than in age-matched controls, and there was a doubling of interstitial connective tissue. Other reports of kidney damage followed, and inevitably the question of the safety of lithium therapy had eventually to be posed​.

The editorial article “Lithium and the kidney scare” [5] noted that the two 1977 reports [6], [7]:

made a profound impression on the psychiatric world. There was a drastic fall in the number of patients started on lithium and many patients were taken off lithium treatment on which they had done well. This resulted in relapses, and suicides are known to have occurred.

Dr. Amdi Amdisen, in a personal communication to Johnson [3, p. 128], explained what happened next:

The ‘kidney scare’ was a panic reaction among psychiatrists which was unreasonably hysterical and undoubtedly caused by insufficient knowledge about the pathology of the kidneys: an exaggerated acute reaction which currently is on its way to the opposite unreasonable reaction, namely a pooh-pooh of the lithium-produced kidney impairments – the latter again because of missing competence concerning nephrology.

Most psychiatrists interested in lithium have not fully recognized that it is not the polyuria or the concentrating ability alone, or the histopathological changes in the kidneys alone, which raise the consideration, but the combination of reduced renal concentrating ability and the interstitial nephropathy. Our opinion is still the same as it was in 1976-1977. The chronic renal toxicity of lithium as it is currently used requires certain, rather limited, extra control procedures. But there was no reason and there is no reason, for either panic or hysteria.

The ”extra control procedures” were laid out by Dr. Per Vestergaard in Chapter 38 of the 1980 Handbook of Lithium Therapy [4, p. 355]:

Guidelines for prophylaxis against lithium-induced functional and morphological renal impairment are difficult to formulate, because we know so little about the relative significance of different treatment factors. The way lithium is administered may, however, be of importance. It seems wise to decrease the exposure to a potentially toxic drug, but opinions differ as to how this is best realized. The following recommendations are therefore not based entirely on existing scientific evidence. Lithium may be administered as slow-release tablets in divided doses, two or three per day, depending on the size of the dose, in order to keep daily peak concentrations in serum and urine low, and vigorous control of serum lithium levels must be exerted in order to avoid toxic levels and intoxications. Efforts should be made to keep serum lithium at the lowest possible level at which effective prophylaxis against relapses can be maintained.

In Chapter 22 by Dr. Amdisen [4, p. 187], an explanation is given for the absence of a Single Daily Dosing (SDD)regimen:

It should be observed that the single-dose schedule gives substantially high peak concentrations and that there is good reason to assume that such extreme lithium concentrations carry with them an extra risk of impairment of the distal parts of the nephron

Given the scientific evidence available at the time, reducing the acute peak daily concentration through multiple daily dosing and keeping the mean daily dosage as low as possible seemed to make the most sense.

It wasn’t until 1981, when evidence first appeared suggesting that low concentrations of lithium might provide the kidneys with a chance to regenerate from any lithium-induced damage. Plenge, Mellerup, and Norgaard monitored how two different ways of giving rats lithium affected their kidneys[10]. Their experiment is summarized by Plenge et al. [9] in 1982:

one group of rats was given their daily lithium in the food, whereas the other had the same amount of lithium injected intraperitoneally every day. The two different routes of administration led to different courses of the serum lithium concentration with a smoother lithium curve in the lithium fed rats; whereas in the lithium injected rats a high peak shortly after the injection was followed by an exponential decrease to low serum lithium concentrations before the next injection. The structural and functional changes in the kidneys were much more pronounced in the lithium fed than in the lithium injected rats, leading to the conclusion that in order to maintain kidney structure and function in lithium treated rats it is important regularly to reach lithium concentrations low enough to allow regenerative processes to occur without interference from lithium

Analogous to the rats' intraperitoneal vs. fed conditions, patients on once-daily regimens will have a serum concentration curve with higher peaks but lower troughs compared to patients on a twice-daily regimen. Fig. 1 from Lauritsen et al. [11] illustrates the pharmacokinetic curves of both regimens. The Copenhagen patients were put on a once-daily dose regimen, while the Aarhus patients were on a twice-daily dose regimen.

Studies, therefore, focused on whether the decreased functional change in kidneys found in injected rats vs fed ones could also be found in humans on SDD regimens compared with MDD counterparts. In a 1981 study by Perry et al. [8], the authors noted a significant decrease in 24-hour urine output for patients on a single daily dose regimen compared to a multiple daily dosing regimen. Still, they made no mention that the regeneration of kidneys due to low lithium serum concentration might be the cause. In 1982, Plenge et al. [9] conducted a similar study between two groups of patients on either single or multiple daily dose regimens. However, they conducted percutaneous kidney biopsies and measured 24-hour urine volumes. They found that:

A considerable scatter of individual values in both groups is seen, but both urine volume and changes in kidney structure were significantly increased in the patients given lithium in divided doses compared with the patients given their whole dose of lithium at night

Remarking:

It thus seems that the conclusion from the rat experiment is valid also for humans treated with lithium, i.e. the importance of regularly reaching serum lithium levels sufficiently low to allow regenerative processes to occur without interference from the lithium.

From the early 1980s onwards, SDD was compared against MDD in several studies in an attempt to determine which regimen produced greater benefits and fewer drawbacks (see Carter et al. [12] and references therein). Around the late 2000’s, review papers assessing the aforementioned studies began recommending patients be put on SDD regimens [13], [14], [15]. The main reasons are summed up in Carter et al. [12]:

Overall, the available evidence is insufficient and inconclusive as to whether SDD of lithium reduces polyuria or other renal effects when compared with MDD. However, no trial has demonstrated any downfall of SDD regarding prophylactic efficacy or adverse effects. Given the added benefits of SDD, such as improved compliance and possibly a reduction in the use of hypnotic medications, we recommend that all patients taking lithium should be assessed and considered for SDD administered at bedtime as soon as possible in their course of therapy.

This recommendation has been slowly adopted into more widespread clinical practice [16].

However, open questions remain. The worry about acute renal effects from daily high peak serum concentrations was not the only reason multiple daily dosing became standard practice. As Dr. Amdisen mentions in Chapter 22 of the Handbook of Lithium Therapy [4, p. 187]:

the placing and the size of the therapeutic window…[is] based on patients using multiple-dose regimens and [is] therefore invalid for the single-dose schedule.

The recommended therapeutic range of lithium has changed over the years [17], [18] and is still debated today [19]. Nevertheless, a therapeutic range for SDD has yet to be outlined [20]. Perhaps more importantly, the acute toxicity suspicion 12 h SLi level of < 1.5 mmol/L [22] (where patients that have 12-hour levels above 1.5 mmol/L should be monitored more carefully for acute toxicity symptoms) is also based on MDD, where peak concentrations are much smaller than their single-dose regimen counterparts.

If once daily dosing is fully adopted in the future, what should the 12-hour serum concentration therapeutic range be? Further, what SDD 12-hour level should be used to indicate potential acute toxicity?

In a 2021 Psychiatric Times article [23], Dr. David Osser asks what I think is probably the most interesting question:

Why doesn’t the higher peak lithium level associated with a large once-daily dose harm the kidneys?

I have not yet found a detailed exploration of this curiosity in the academic literature.

Thanks, all for reading. To subscribe to this newsletter, click here!
